endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Identify when clinicians and staff need to be trained on specific AI solutions prior to implementation

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions: Lifecycle Management and Marketing Submission Recommendations (draft guidance)
endorsements.quote: A description of the intended users, their characteristics, and the level and type of training 381 they are expected to have and/or receive.

endorsements.title: Developing, purchasing, implementing and monitoring AI tools in radiology: practical considerations. A multi-society statement
endorsements.issuer: ACR, CAR, ESR, RANZCR, RSNA; Radiol Artif Intell 2024 (PMID 38251899, doi:10.1148/ryai.230513)
endorsements.quote: How do users need to be trained and which psychological effects need to be considered with regard to human-AI-interaction?

endorsements.title: Responsible Use of AI in Healthcare (RUAIH) guidance
endorsements.issuer: The Joint Commission and Coalition for Health AI
endorsements.quote: Healthcare organizations should, at a minimum, define and document how users of the AI system will be given relevant AI tool and system documentation and role-specific training to ensure that AI systems are used and monitored appropriately, safely, and effectively.

commentary.bottom_line: Four sources endorse assessing and documenting AI tool training needs by user role before implementation, but no study tests whether this practice improves user preparedness or patient outcomes. No study documents the hazard of deploying tools without defined training requirements, so the recommendation currently rests on expert consensus alone.

perspectives.view: No study tests pre-implementation training-needs assessment, and no study measures how often tools reach users without defined training. The four endorsements come from one framework and three guidance documents, which reflects expert agreement rather than tested effect. Under GRADE conventions, consensus statements do not supply a certainty rating for an intervention's effect.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software asks manufacturers to describe intended users and the level and type of training they are expected to have or receive. A health system could draw on that submission content at intake, although the guidance remains a draft and does not direct deployers to document training needs.

The radiology multi-society statement pairs training with psychological effects of human-AI interaction, and the RUAIH guidance calls for role-specific training and documentation. Neither source reports how much staff time such assessments require or whether documented training plans are carried out with fidelity in practice.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should compare deployments with and without a documented, role-specific training-needs assessment at intake. They should measure user competence, appropriate reliance on AI output, error rates, and staff time. Descriptive studies should also estimate how often AI tools are currently deployed without defined training requirements.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy settings. Safety-net systems may have fewer training staff and more staff turnover, and whether intake-stage training assessments work under those conditions is unknown.
